sysd-blocks-190.q: Why does putting a reverse proxy in front of back ends create both an availability risk and a security risk?
sysd-blocks-190.a: It is a single point of failure: misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable. To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic it must decrypt and re-encrypt it, which needs the TLS certificate and private key and makes it a more valuable attack target.

sysd-blocks-136.q: Which is still useful with only one server, a reverse proxy or a load balancer, and which can stand in for the other?
sysd-blocks-136.a: A reverse proxy is useful even with one server and can also act as a load balancer, but not the other way around. A load balancer is useful when multiple servers serve the same function.

sysd-blocks-002.q: Why does video and audio streaming usually have a hit ratio near zero, and what does that do to an LRU cache?
sysd-blocks-002.a: Each bit of the stream is read once (a compulsory miss), used, and never read or written again. LRU in particular lets streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again, which is called cache pollution.

sysd-blocks-005.q: What happens in an LFU cache to an object that was accessed often in the past and then becomes unpopular, and how does LFUDA fix it?
sysd-blocks-005.a: It stays in an LFU cache for a long time, blocking newer or less-popular objects from replacing it. LFU with dynamic aging adds a cache-age factor to the reference count so such objects become eligible for replacement.

sysd-blocks-007.q: Why do CPU caches with large associativity often use pseudo-LRU instead of true LRU?
sysd-blocks-007.a: LRU must track what was used and when, and for caches with large associativity (generally more than four ways) that cost becomes prohibitive. Pseudo-LRU needs only one bit per cache item.

sysd-blocks-015.q: What does a write-back cache risk if the caching layer crashes, and how can that risk be reduced?
sysd-blocks-015.a: It confirms the write as soon as it completes in the caching layer and syncs it to the database asynchronously, so it risks data loss if the caching layer crashes. Having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.

sysd-blocks-029.q: How does a Memcached client decide which server holds a key, and why does that make the design scale?
sysd-blocks-029.a: Each client knows all the servers, and the client library hashes the key to pick one, a simple form of sharding. Because the servers never talk to each other, it is a scalable shared-nothing architecture.

sysd-blocks-014.q: Why can't a general-purpose operating system implement the optimal replacement policy, and what is it still good for?
sysd-blocks-014.a: It needs knowledge of the future to evict the lines that will be reused farthest ahead, and it is generally impossible to predict how far ahead information will be needed. Its practical minimum can still be calculated after experimentation, so it gives a yardstick for comparing the effectiveness of a chosen cache algorithm.

sysd-blocks-009.q: Which access pattern makes MRU beat LRU, and why?
sysd-blocks-009.a: For random access patterns and repeated scans over large datasets, called cyclic access patterns, MRU gets more hits than LRU because it tends to retain older data. It is most useful where the older an item is, the more likely it is to be accessed.

sysd-blocks-161.q: How does ARC adapt to changing usage without keeping the data of recently evicted entries?
sysd-blocks-161.a: Each of its lists gets a ghost list holding only the keys of entries recently evicted from it, never their data. A hit in B1 grows the target size of T1 and a hit in B2 shrinks it, which also decides whether T1 or T2 gives up an entry when the cache is full.

sysd-blocks-024.q: Why can the expiry of a heavily requested cached page bring a system down?
sysd-blocks-024.a: When the cached page expires under very heavy load, many threads across the server farm all try to render it at the same time, and none of them knows the others are doing so. That concurrent load can exhaust shared resources and cause congestion collapse, so every attempt to re-render times out and the cache hit rate drops to zero.

sysd-blocks-018.q: What happens if a malicious user floods the system with queries for keys that exist in neither the cache nor the database, and how can the cache help?
sysd-blocks-018.a: Because the database has nothing to return, the application cannot populate the cache, which puts heavy pressure on both the cache and the database, so the database can easily be overloaded. One fix is to cache a null value for such keys with a short TTL; another is a Bloom filter, which stops queries for keys it says do not exist from reaching the cache or the database.

sysd-blocks-026.a: It does not help when accessing the cache takes as long as accessing the primary data store, or when requests have low repetition, because caching performance comes from repeated access patterns. It also does not help when data changes frequently, because the cached version gets out of sync and the primary data store must be accessed every time.

sysd-blocks-033.q: How does banning cached content differ from purging it?
sysd-blocks-033.a: Purge removes content, including all its variants, from the caching proxy immediately. Ban adds a reference to the cached content to a ban list that requests are checked against, and on a match new content is fetched, returned and cached, so unlike purge it removes nothing at once.

sysd-blocks-069.q: Why is blocking a single source not enough to stop a distributed denial-of-service attack?
sysd-blocks-069.a: In a DDoS the flood comes from many sources, often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking one source does not stop it and more sophisticated mitigation is needed.

sysd-blocks-070.q: Why does a peer-to-peer content network keep the original distributor's setup and running costs very small?
sysd-blocks-070.a: Unlike client-server systems, it can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share. That property makes the setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor.

sysd-blocks-077.q: Why do telco CDNs have a built-in cost advantage over traditional CDNs?
sysd-blocks-077.a: Traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs, while telco CDNs own the last mile and operate their own delivery infrastructure.

sysd-blocks-072.q: Which kind of site suits a pull CDN rather than a push CDN, and why?
sysd-blocks-072.a: Heavy-traffic sites suit a pull CDN, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN. Push CDNs suit sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.

sysd-blocks-081.q: Why can locating a client by its resolver's IP route it badly, and what does the edns-client-subnet option change?
sysd-blocks-081.a: A client that uses a non-local resolver that is far away gets poor performance when the CDN locates it by the resolver's IP. With the edns-client-subnet EDNS0 option, CDNs use the IP address of the requesting client's subnet instead, which drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers.

sysd-blocks-178.q: How does Subresource Integrity keep a tampered CDN-hosted script from running in a page?
sysd-blocks-178.a: The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location, and the browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match. A page therefore loads only a script whose content matches the hash the site author references.

sysd-blocks-035.q: What do many NoSQL systems trade away to gain speed and availability?
sysd-blocks-035.a: Many follow the BASE model, prioritizing speed and availability over strict consistency through eventual consistency: updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale. Most also lack full ACID transaction support, sacrificing it for performance and scalability.

sysd-blocks-061.q: Why does a graph database pull ahead of a relational one as relationships get deeper?
sysd-blocks-061.a: Relational databases need many joins over several tables for complex relationships, while a graph database follows stored links and avoids costly joins. Its advantage grows with query depth and complexity.

sysd-blocks-060.q: Why must a bank transfer be handled as a single transaction?
sysd-blocks-060.a: It requires subtracting the amount from one account and adding the same amount to the other, and a transaction must be atomic, meaning it completes or has no effect.

sysd-blocks-055.q: What do you gain and what do you lose by choosing a higher isolation level?
sysd-blocks-055.a: A higher isolation level reduces the concurrency effects users may meet, but it needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another. A lower level lets more users access the same data at once but increases effects such as dirty reads or lost updates.

sysd-blocks-045.q: Why do analytics databases favor column-oriented storage while operational databases favor row-oriented storage?
sysd-blocks-045.a: Analytic access usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows, so analytics databases benefit from column-oriented DBMSs, while operational databases benefit from row-oriented ones.

sysd-blocks-052.q: Why do star schemas deliberately relax normalization?
sysd-blocks-052.a: Relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic and reporting, faster read-only queries and aggregations, fewer joins per query, and an efficient source for OLAP cubes.

sysd-blocks-066.q: Why is an ordinary index a poor fit for spatial queries, and what do spatial databases use instead?
sysd-blocks-066.a: Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions. Spatial databases use a spatial index designed for multi-dimensional ordering, and the R-tree is typically the preferred one.

sysd-blocks-169.q: What does ROLAP gain and what does it give up compared with MOLAP?
sysd-blocks-169.a: ROLAP scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool. It is generally slower than MOLAP, and its aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

sysd-blocks-067.q: Why does copying values such as a username into each record only suit workloads where reads are much more common than writes?
sysd-blocks-067.a: Instead of storing only foreign keys, this approach stores the actual foreign values with the data so no further lookup is needed. But copied values must be changed in many places when they change, so it works better when reads are much more common than writes.

sysd-blocks-053.q: Why can forcing one database to satisfy every requirement backfire, and what does using several databases cost?
sysd-blocks-053.a: Forcing one database to satisfy every requirement can yield a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none solution, because different databases solve different problems. Knitting several database products together has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

sysd-blocks-057.q: What happens when a step errors in an ACID database compared with a BASE database?
sysd-blocks-057.a: An ACID database fails the whole transaction if any step errors. A BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later.

sysd-blocks-171.q: Why did financial and order-processing systems turn to NewSQL?
sysd-blocks-171.a: They outgrew conventional relational databases but needed transactional guarantees that NoSQL could not give. The old options were bigger computers or custom distribution middleware, both costly, and NewSQL tries to reconcile this.

sysd-blocks-063.q: How does multiversion concurrency control keep readers from waiting for writers?
sysd-blocks-063.a: An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting, so each user sees a snapshot of the database at one instant and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits. Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID, so reads and writes are isolated without locks and writers do not block readers.

sysd-blocks-165.q: What rule must a transaction follow under two-phase locking, and what does obeying it guarantee?
sysd-blocks-165.a: Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired, so a transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one. Schedules that obey this rule are serializable.

sysd-blocks-042.q: Under snapshot isolation, how can two concurrent withdrawals each pass a balance check and still leave the accounts in deficit?
sysd-blocks-042.a: Each transaction checks the rule against its own snapshot, so with two concurrent $200 withdrawals both commit and the total ends at -$200; this is write skew, which snapshot isolation permits. Under serializability it is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other.

sysd-blocks-182.q: Why does a write-ahead log let a database avoid flushing its data pages at every commit?
sysd-blocks-182.a: The central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the WAL records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. So after a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the WAL, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO.

sysd-blocks-186.q: How does an inverted index differ from a forward index, and why does that make full-text search practical?
sysd-blocks-186.a: A forward index stores the list of words per document, and inverting it gives the inverted index, which lists the documents per word. Without it a query would iterate through every word of every document, which is often not technically realistic; with it, the query jumps to the word by random access.

sysd-blocks-105.q: Why can a B+ tree handle range queries and ordered iteration better than a B-tree?
sysd-blocks-105.a: Its leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient. A B-tree cannot build such a list because not all its keys are in the leaves.

sysd-blocks-107.q: Why might denormalizing a design by hand perform worse than the normalized design?
sysd-blocks-107.a: Denormalizing by hand can match the query speed, but the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints, which slow writes. Under heavy write load it may therefore perform worse than the normalized design.
